Who keeps property records in Miami-Dade County?

The Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller is the county recorder. Under Chapter 28 of the Florida Statutes, the clerk is the official recorder of every instrument that law allows to be recorded here.

The Official Records hold deeds, mortgages, liens, certain affidavits, subdivision plats, judgments, declarations of domicile, satisfactions and releases, powers of attorney and financial statements. Fees and transfer taxes are figured and collected when a document is recorded.

How do I search Miami-Dade Official Records?

Use the clerk's online Official Records search, which covers all of the instruments above. A search by name or by book and page finds the document you need.

  • Name searches work for grantors, grantees and lienholders.
  • Credit bureaus pick up liens and judgments recorded here. If a bureau reports one you do not recognize, ask them for its book and page and request a copy from the Records Library.
  • The clerk also runs a free fraud alert that notifies an owner within a day whenever a deed or mortgage is filed against the owner's name.

Which fees does the Miami-Dade clerk charge?

Most documents cost $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page. A lis pendens costs $5 for the first page and $4 for each additional page.

How do the state fee rules compare with the clerk's list?

Florida's clerk fee statute lists $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches, plus $1.00 for each name beyond four. It adds a $1.00 modernization charge on the first page and $0.50 on later pages, and an extra $4 per page for technology.

Plats cost $30.00 for the first page and $15.00 for each added page under the statute, and processing a tax deed application costs $60.00. The Miami-Dade clerk lists its own all-in figures, which is why the county's first-page fee reads $10.

Quote the clerk's current schedule to your title agent rather than adding statute lines yourself.

How much documentary stamp tax applies to a deed?

The clerk prints deed stamps at 60 cents per $100 of consideration, rounded up to the next hundred. Florida's revenue department confirms that Miami-Dade is the one county that uses 60 cents instead of the standard 70.

A separate surtax of 45 cents per $100 applies to transfers of real property other than a single-family residence. Mortgages pay 35 cents per $100 of the note, plus intangible tax of $2 per $1,000.

All parties to a deed are liable for the tax under state rules, regardless of who agrees to pay. Your contract with the buyer sets the practical split.

What goes on a mortgage, satisfaction or lien filing?

Mortgage filings must be original, signed and notarized. Attach a copy of the note, or write the note amount across the face of the mortgage. It needs addresses for lender and borrower and a Prepared By line.

  • A satisfaction or release needs the book and page of the mortgage, the holder's signature and a notarized acknowledgement.
  • An assignment of mortgage needs the book and page, the assignor's signature and a notary.
  • A construction lien needs the lienor's signature, a notary and a legal description or property address.

A seller paying off a loan should confirm the satisfaction is recorded, then search the Official Records to see it indexed.

How do special deeds and court sales show up in Miami-Dade records?

A quit claim deed, a deed given in place of foreclosure and a contract for deed are all on the revenue department's list of taxable documents. The revenue department treats an executor's deed under a probated will as not taxable.

A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. A lis pendens, the notice that a foreclosure suit is pending, records at $5 for the first page, so searching for one early can warn a buyer that a lender has gone to court.

Any buyer or seller in a distressed transfer should pull the title record before signing so every lien is in view.

What must a Miami-Dade deed include to be accepted?

The clerk's deed checklist is specific, and a missing item gets a document returned.

  • An original document with the seller's signature.
  • Addresses for grantors and grantees.
  • Two witnesses not related to the transaction, with each name and post office address printed beneath the signature.
  • A full notary acknowledgement.
  • A Prepared By statement with name and address.
  • Documentary stamps, plus the property transfer form.
  • A folio number, which is encouraged but not required, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Section 689.01 of the Florida Statutes separately requires two subscribing witnesses on a conveyance.

What are my options for filing a document in person, by mail or electronically?

The clerk gives four routes for filing. Bring the original and fees to the Osvaldo N. Soto Miami-Dade Justice Center, mail it to the Office of County Recorder at 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, FL 33128, use an approved eRecording vendor, or use the clerk's eRecording Web Service for Notices of Commencement and Declarations of Domicile.

Electronic filings, which the clerk says it cannot promise to process the same day, take roughly 1 to 3 business days, excluding weekends and holidays, before they appear online. The clerk says it cannot promise same-day recording, so bring time-sensitive documents in person.

Cash is accepted only in person. Credit cards are in person only, with a $5,000 daily limit.

Can I remove a Social Security number from a public record?

Yes. The clerk lets you request redaction of Social Security, bank account and credit card numbers from documents that are available online, using its online redaction form with the file number or book and page.

People covered by Chapter 119 exemptions can file a confidentiality request, in person or online. Party names stay in the index unless the name includes a street address, as in some trusts or LLCs.

How does the county's size affect recording and searching?

Miami-Dade has 975,411 households and 1,125,274 housing units, and Census data show 88.0 percent of residents had not changed address within a year. The county issued 16,535 building permits in 2025.

A county that large produces a heavy filing load, so a clean document matters. The clerk's checklist makes witness addresses and the notary block mandatory, and the clerk states it cannot guarantee same-day recording.

Search by every spelling of a name, and add the folio number when you have it, since the clerk encourages including it.

More questions about Miami-Dade County, FL Property Records

Where do I file a deed in Miami-Dade?

At the County Recorder's Office, 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, or by an approved eRecording vendor. The clerk accepts mail and in-person filings as well.

What does the clerk charge to file a Miami-Dade deed?

The clerk lists $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, before documentary stamps. Statute section 28.24(13) prints a base of $5.00 and $4.00 per page and allows other charges on top, so use the clerk's list.

Does Miami-Dade charge a deed surtax on a house?

The 45 cents per $100 surtax applies to real property other than a single-family residence, so a deed for only a single-family home does not carry it.

Do I have to record a deed after a sale?

Recording is how the buyer gets public notice of the transfer. Ask the title agent to record promptly, and search Official Records afterward to confirm the deed appears.

How long does eRecording take in Miami-Dade?

Roughly 1 to 3 business days before the document is viewable online, per the clerk.

Where do I search Broward County property records?

Use the Official Records search on the Broward County Records, Taxes and Treasury Division site. It is an Acclaim-based system that opens with a disclaimer you must accept.

You can search nine ways: party name (grantor or grantee), book and page, document type, instrument number, case number, consideration range, date recorded, a simple search with plain-language prompts such as a copy of your deed, and parcel ID. The simple search is a good first stop for a seller who only wants to know whether any liens have been filed against them.

How far back do Broward Official Records go online?

Documents recorded from July 7, 1977 forward are fully searchable. Plats and maps are searchable regardless of date.

Older records need other methods, as the county explains:

  • March 9, 1972 through July 7, 1977: searchable only by instrument number, book type and book and page range, or record date.
  • Before March 9, 1972: not available on the site.

For a Broward house that has been in a family since the 1960s, expect the chain of title to need an in-person request or a title company search for the oldest links.

Who is the recorder in Broward County?

In Broward the recording office sits within the county's Records, Taxes and Treasury Division, with questions answered at 954-831-4000. Confirm the office and the amount due before you mail a deed.

The division also offers bulk data. It provides 10 continuous days of Official Records files at no charge, with images and index data, and it lists electronic recording vendors for firms that file many documents. A single homeowner rarely needs either, but a title company handling your Broward closing may use e-recording.

What does it cost to file a deed in Broward County?

Florida sets the clerk charges by statute, and the table shows the lines in s. 28.24(13). Confirm the total with the Broward recording office, since other charges can be added.

What stamp tax does a Broward deed carry?

Broward uses the standard state rate of a rate of $0.70 for every $100 of the price and debt transferred. Miami-Dade next door has its own rates, and Broward does not share them.

Mortgages on the property count as consideration even if the buyer does not assume them. Each party is liable, whatever the contract says about who pays. An unrecorded deed is taxable too.

  • Taxable examples: warranty, special warranty, quit claim and trustee's deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure and certificates of title.
  • Exempt examples: spousal homestead deeds where a mortgage is the only consideration, and divorce deeds for the marital home.
  • Lady bird deeds: a 2020 Department of Revenue advisement found one not subject to the tax on the facts presented, because no present beneficial interest passed.

How can I protect a Broward owner from deed fraud?

The Broward County Property Appraiser runs a free Owner Alert service. It notifies subscribers when the appraiser's office receives a document changing the ownership of their property.

The service only watches for ownership changes, so it suits a seller who is moving away or a family holding an inherited house that sits empty. The appraiser also points to its FAQ page for questions about recording a deed, adding or removing an owner and getting copies of recorded documents. Search for the word deed in the questions box, then pick the topic that fits your situation, such as adding or removing an owner.

What happens to property taxes after a Broward sale?

The appraiser states that a change of ownership resets assessed value to full market value, which can raise the new owner's taxes. A Save Our Homes cap that protected a long-time seller does not travel with the house.

The appraiser does not send bills or collect tax. Billing and collection belong to the Broward County Tax Collector, whose appraiser-listed contact is (954) 357-4829 and revenue@browardtax.org. Portability lets a seller carry part of the homestead benefit to a new Florida home if the new homestead is established within three years of the first of January in the year the old one was abandoned.

How do liens and foreclosures show up in Broward records?

Search by party name and by parcel ID, because liens attach to the property and to the person. A court sale ends in a certificate of title, and ten quiet days confirm it (s. 45.031).

A tax deed buyer must apply after two years from April 1 of the certificate year, and the tax collector lists everyone to be notified, including mortgagees and contract-for-deed vendees (s. 197.502).

How is a Broward deed filed after closing?

A title company can file the deed electronically through one of the vendors the county lists for electronic recording. A seller doing it by hand should call 954-831-4000 first.

Check three things before filing: the grantor name matches the last recorded deed, the legal description is copied exactly, and the two required witnesses signed (s. 689.01). The deed is taxable whether or not it is recorded, so skipping the filing does not avoid the stamp tax.

  • Gather the parcel ID from the appraiser site.
  • Prepare the recording charges and stamp tax in the amounts the office quotes.
  • Keep the instrument number once it is recorded, since the Broward search supports instrument number lookups and you will need it for any later copy.

How do records help with an inherited Broward house?

Search the decedent under every name variation, including nicknames and married names, and look for unreleased mortgages. Plats and maps are searchable at every date range, so a lot-line question can be checked there. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable for stamp tax, and Florida has had no estate tax for deaths after 2004.

Summary administration may fit an estate of $150,000 or less in non-exempt assets, or an owner dead more than two years (s. 735.201). Creditor claims face a cutoff set by s. 733.702. Expect the title insurer to want these steps finished first.

What can a foreclosure mean for a Broward title search?

A lender may use the order-to-show-cause route under s. 702.10, where the hearing waits for the later of 20 days after the order is served or 45 days after the complaint is served. Look for a certificate of title if a sale has already happened.

Owner-occupied homes are carved out of the quick payment-or-vacate order, and a homestead exemption on the latest roll is a rebuttable presumption of owner occupancy.

More questions about Broward County, FL Property Records

Where is the Broward County recording office?

It is the Records, Taxes and Treasury Division of Broward County, reachable at 954-831-4000. The Official Records search is hosted on its own site.

Are all Broward deeds searchable online?

No. Documents from July 7, 1977 forward are fully searchable. Records from March 9, 1972 to July 7, 1977 need an instrument number, book and page, or record date, and earlier ones are not on the site.

What is the Florida deed stamp rate in Broward?

It is a rate of $0.70 for every $100 of the price and debt transferred under s. 201.02. Every party is liable, and it is collected at filing.

Is there a free alert for deed filings on my Broward home?

Yes. The Broward County Property Appraiser offers Owner Alert, which notifies you when a document changing ownership of your property reaches that office.

Does my assessment cap pass to the buyer?

No. A change of ownership resets assessed value to just value the next first of January, per the Florida Department of Revenue. Exceptions cover things like transfers between spouses.

Where are Hillsborough County property records kept?

Hillsborough County deeds, mortgages and liens sit in the Official Records, run by the Clerk of Court and Comptroller. The clerk's recording department says about 25 million documents have been recorded since 1846, with roughly 2,000 new ones added each day.

The index from 1965 to the present can be searched free online through the clerk's Official Records public search. Older material sits in the Official Records Library, where the earliest items date back to 1836, and the clerk also hosts an archive with deed indexes from 1948 to 1957 and Official Records indexes from 1958 to 1966. Subdivision plats, tax rolls from 1883 to the present and judgments are also kept there. Library staff will search records and prepare a Clerk's Certificate for a fee, and a Declaration of Domicile is recorded for $10 at Room 140, 401 Pierce Street in Tampa.

How do I search Hillsborough County Official Records for a house?

Search by the owner's name, then read the instrument list for deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, liens and easements. A clean search before a sale shows who holds title and which loans or claims still sit against it.

  • Start with the current owner's name and work backward through each deed.
  • Look for a recorded satisfaction for every mortgage you expect to be paid off.
  • Check for lien filings, easements and notices of commencement from recent work.
  • Order a certified copy when a lender or title company asks for one.

Copies cost $1.00 per page, and certification adds $2.00 per document. The clerk offers self-validating electronic certified copies around the clock through eCertify, delivered as a PDF by email. An in-person request through the Records Library costs $2 for each year searched, $1 per page and $2 for certifying.

Which fees apply when a Hillsborough County deed is recorded?

On the clerk's page the first page of a recording is $10.00 and later pages are $8.50 apiece; four names are included, and every name past four adds $1.00. Section 28.24 of the state statutes builds those totals from a $5.00 base for page one and $4.00 for later pages, plus a modernization charge and a $4 per page technology charge.

The clerk offers an online Deed Calculator for a full figure, including the state tax collected at recording. Florida Revenue says the clerk collects it at recording and that every party to the deed owes it, whichever side agrees to pay.

What are the Hillsborough County witness rules for recording a deed?

Since January 1, 2024, deeds and similar instruments need two witnesses, each with a printed name and a post office address. The clerk says the address has to be a physical address or a post office box, and an email address will not do.

Florida's conveyance statute also requires a conveyance of land to be in writing and signed in the presence of two witnesses. Under section 695.26 a document missing the required witness information, and a rejected document is returned with a notice of rejection. The rule covers deeds, easements, affidavits of interest in land and agreements, notices or memorandums for deed.

  • Print or type each witness's name and address legibly next to the signature.
  • Have the signed, notarized original ready; the clerk accepts it over the counter or in the mail only.
  • Attach a transmittal form or cover letter and a prepaid return envelope.

How fast can a Hillsborough County document be recorded?

Only recording in person guarantees same-day service. Documents mailed or sent through an e-recording vendor are processed in the order received, and the clerk does not promise same-day or next-day recording for them.

The recording department accepts documents by mail at P.O. Box 3249 in Tampa, in person at the Downtown Tampa, Brandon and Plant City locations, and through a list of e-recording vendors the clerk publishes as a courtesy without endorsing any of them. The phone number printed for the office is (813) 276-8100. For a closing with a deadline, have the title company record in person or through its own e-recording account. A consumer portal also exists for notices of commencement only, and a mailed notice of commencement can take up to 7 business days to be validated and indexed.

Which Hillsborough County records matter at a sale?

The deed chain, open mortgages, recorded liens and any easement or notice of commencement decide how smoothly a Hillsborough County closing runs. The title company reads the same index before issuing a policy, so a lien you find first is a lien you can pay off first.

  • Deed correction: the clerk suggests a real property attorney for adding, removing or fixing a name, and the recording fee is $10.00 first page and $8.50 each added page.
  • Quitclaim: Florida statute 689.025 contains a quit claim form, but the clerk says deputies cannot offer legal advice and that a quitclaim may not suit every transaction.
  • Lost deed: buy a certified copy through eCertify.
  • Privacy: a social security number can be redacted from an image on the clerk's website on written request, at no charge.

Death certificates, military discharges and family or probate court papers cannot be shown on the clerk's public website under section 28.2221. A web subscription at $100 a year gives access to those images for eligible users.

How do Hillsborough County records connect to property tax?

The recorded deed starts a chain that ends on the tax bill. Once a deed is recorded, the property appraiser updates the owner on the roll, and the Hillsborough County Tax Collector's bills follow that ownership.

Under state rules, a sale or other transfer of title resets the assessment to just value the following January 1, with spouse transfers and some transfers at death excepted. DOR also lists deeds in lieu of foreclosure, quit claim deeds and contracts for deed as taxable documents. Florida Revenue adds that a deed is taxable whether or not it is recorded, and tax on an unrecorded taxable document is paid to the state instead of the clerk. A deed signed by a personal representative under a probated will is listed as not taxable. For the bill itself, see our Hillsborough County property tax guide.

More questions about Hillsborough County, FL Property Records

Where do I search Hillsborough County property records?

Use the Official Records public search run by the Hillsborough County Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller. The index from 1965 forward is free online, and older records are handled through the Official Records Library.

What are the recording charges for a Hillsborough County deed?

The clerk prints $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, with $1.00 for each name after the first four. Deed documentary stamp tax is separate, at a rate of 70 cents for each $100 paid.

Does the Hillsborough clerk take deeds by email?

No. The clerk takes the original signed and notarized deed in person or by mail, and not by email. E-recording through a vendor is another route, though the clerk cannot promise same-day recording for it.

What witness information must a Hillsborough County deed include?

Two witnesses, each with a printed name and a physical or post office box address. Documents missing that information can be rejected, and an email address is not accepted as the witness address.

Where do I order a certified Hillsborough deed copy?

The clerk's eCertify service sells certified copies online at any hour and emails a PDF, and the office also takes requests in person. Certification adds $2.00 per document to the $1.00 per page copy charge.

What does the Orange County Official Records system hold?

The Orange County Comptroller's Official Records Department records, indexes and archives the documents that make up the county's Official Records. Its own description lists deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, claims of lien, final judgments and orders, notices of commencement and declarations of domicile.

For a seller in Orange County, this is the place where the paper trail on a house lives. Before closing, the buyer's title agent will comb it for any mortgage, lien or judgment tied to your name or parcel. Reading the same index yourself, before you list, shows what that agent is going to find.

  • Deeds and mortgages that show who owns the parcel and who lent against it
  • Satisfactions that show a loan was paid off and released
  • Claims of lien, which can come from contractors or associations and must be cleared before a clean sale
  • Final judgments recorded against an owner
  • Notices of commencement, which signal recent construction work

Who keeps which Orange County records?

Recorded land documents sit with the Orange County Comptroller, while a different office runs the circuit and county court case files. In Florida the clerk of the circuit court is the officer who records documents and collects documentary stamp tax at recording, and in Orange County the Comptroller's Official Records Department carries out that recording work.

The Property Appraiser is a third office. It keeps the ownership, value and exemption record for each parcel, and its home page offers property search, a tax estimator, forms and tax roll information. The Tax Collector bills and collects the tax. If a question is about a recorded deed or lien, start with the Comptroller. Use the Official Records page on the Comptroller's website at occompt.com, then run the index search by owner name or by the legal description of the parcel. Search every name that has ever been on the deed, including a spouse or a trust, because a lien recorded against a former owner can still sit on the chain of title.

Compare what you find with the Property Appraiser's parcel record, so the legal description, the owner of record and homestead status line up. A mismatch between a mailing address, a surname or a legal description is easier to fix before you have a buyer waiting. If a recorded item looks wrong or unfamiliar, ask the Comptroller's Official Records Department how to get a certified copy, and ask a title company or a Florida attorney what it means for your sale.

The Official Records index is a finding aid. Treat a search screen as a lead to the recorded instrument, and get a certified copy from the Comptroller when a lender, court or title agent needs a formal one.

A filing adds up from page charges plus documentary stamp tax, and the stamp tax usually outweighs the page charges. The state deed rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and only Miami-Dade runs a different schedule, so Orange County uses the standard rate.

The Department of Revenue adds that every party to the document is on the hook whoever agrees to pay, and the tax is gathered at the recording counter. Consideration counts money, the discharge of an obligation and any mortgage or encumbrance, whether or not the buyer assumes it.

You scan the document and upload it through the vendor's application. The original never leaves your hands, and funds for transfer taxes, recording fees and a small vendor fee move by ACH. What happens to a deed on tax certificate or tax deed property?

If taxes stay unpaid, the Tax Collector sells a tax certificate, and a certificate left unredeemed for two years can lead to a tax deed application. The Tax Collector's site says tax deed sales in Orange County are processed through the Comptroller's Office, and the Comptroller's page confirms that tax deed auctions are performed by the Official Records Department.

State statute says the clerk holds the public auction, that the high bidder posts a nonrefundable deposit of 5 percent of the bid or $200, whichever is greater, and that the rest of the money plus recording charges is due within 24 hours, excluding weekends and holidays. An owner behind on taxes should settle with the Tax Collector well before this stage. Just over 56 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the five-year survey puts the middle home value at $390,100. All of this sits on 902.02 square miles of land. That mix of owners, renters and new construction explains why searches here often turn up notices of commencement, association liens and several mortgages on one chain of title.

How can an Orange County seller use the records to sell faster?

Pull your own records first, then clear what you can. A recorded mortgage with no matching satisfaction, an old contractor claim or an unreleased judgment can each stall a closing for weeks.

  • Search the index under every owner name and any prior spelling
  • Confirm each paid-off loan shows a recorded satisfaction
  • Ask the Property Appraiser to correct a wrong mailing address or exemption record
  • Check with the Tax Collector that no current or past taxes are open
  • Hand your title agent the list so surprises surface early

If the title is messy or you need to sell quickly as is, a direct cash buyer can often work around these items. Compare any offer with the lien payoff figures in your own records.

Use the Orange County Comptroller's Official Records Department. Its page at occompt.com explains the department and links to the record search. Deeds, mortgages, satisfactions and liens are all recorded there.

Which party covers the deed stamps in Orange County?

Every party to the document is liable, in the revenue department's words, whichever side agrees to pay. Your sales contract decides who actually pays. The rate is 70 cents for each $100 of consideration.

Is Orange County's Official Records the same as court records?

No. The Comptroller's Official Records Department keeps recorded instruments such as deeds, liens and recorded judgments. Court case files are kept by the clerk of the courts. Ask the right office for the right record.

Is online filing of a deed possible in Orange County?

Yes, through the approved eRecording vendors the Comptroller lists. You upload a scan, pay taxes and fees by ACH, and documents are typically recorded the same day when sent during regular business hours. The department lists 407-836-5111 for eRecording questions.

Do open tax balances hold up a sale in Orange County?

They matter at closing more than at recording. A bill left past March 31 goes delinquent, and a certificate auction follows by June 1. Have the title agent get the Tax Collector's payoff.

That department answers at (904) 255-2025. Its hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., except holidays. The recording desk is a separate department, reached at (904) 255-2000 with the same hours.

How far back does the Duval online Official Records search go?

The online portal covers documents recorded since 1988, plus marriage licenses recorded since February 1981. Anything older needs a request to the Official Records and Research staff.

For a pre-1988 document, send as much detail as you have, such as party names and dates, in person to Room 1253 or by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope. Viewing and printing uncertified copies from the portal is free, and paper copies from the office cost $1 per page. Certified copies carry the $2.00 certification fee set by Florida law.

  • Payment by mail: money order, business check or cashier's check payable to the Duval Clerk of the Circuit Court. Personal checks are not accepted.
  • E-recording: submissions go through a third-party vendor, and the clerk does not endorse any of them.

The clerk processes documents in the order received but cannot promise same-day or next-day recording for mail or e-recorded items. If timing matters for a closing, record in person at the Recording Department.

What recording taxes apply to a Duval County sale?

Deeds in Duval carry documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration, the rate used everywhere except Miami-Dade. The clerk collects it when the deed is recorded.

Consideration includes money paid, a discharged obligation and any mortgage on the property, assumed or not. A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. Personal representative's deeds under a probated will are listed as not taxable, but the state says there is no exemption for estate planning transfers in general.

Mortgage tax is 35 cents per $100 secured. The statute also sets recording charges of $5.00 for a first page and $4.00 for each added page, with extra per-page modernization and technology charges on top. Ask the recording desk for the all-in figure for your document.

Notice runs for two consecutive weeks, the high bidder posts a 5 percent deposit, and objections are due within 10 days of the certificate of sale. The office charges $2.00 for each year's search, which is small next to a closing delay. Ask the Property Appraiser about homestead status, since the clerk refers those questions out.

How does Duval help owners spot a fake deed?

The clerk offers a free Property Fraud Alert that notifies registered users when a document is recorded in their personal or business name. Scammers record fake deeds to appear as owners and then rent or sell homes that are not theirs.

Vacant houses and inherited homes are the usual targets in a large county like Duval. If you own a rental or an empty property in Jacksonville, sign up before you list it, and recheck the Official Records search whenever a buyer's title company reports something unexpected.

The clerk's records liaison is at 315 Court Street, Room 400, Clearwater, FL 33756, with a phone line at (727) 464-3341. The Customer Information Center number printed on the fee schedule is (727) 464-7000. If a document is not free online, the clerk's copy request center gives a quote.

How big and how dense is Pinellas County?

The county is a peninsula 38 miles long and 15 miles wide at its widest point, with 280 square miles and 588 miles of coastline. The county's own fast facts page calls it the most densely populated county in Florida, at 3,425 residents on each square mile, and the second smallest by land area.

Under section 28.24(13) of the Florida Statutes, page one of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches costs $5.00 and each later page costs $4.00. Extra items include $1.00 per name past four, a modernization trust fund charge of $1.00 plus $0.50 per added page, and a technology charge of $4 per page.

Mail goes to Lee County Clerk of Courts, PO Box 2278, Fort Myers, FL 33902. The clerk's office will not fill out forms for you, and its page suggests hiring a professional experienced in preparing deeds. The legal description must be accurate on every instrument, and the spelling of each name must match the signature block.

What must a Lee County deed contain to be recorded?

The clerk says a deed must meet the requirements of section 695.26 of the Florida Statutes, and its checklist is specific. A rejected deed costs time, so run through it before you sign.

  • A line naming and giving the address of whoever drafted the deed.
  • Printed names and mailing addresses of the grantors (sellers) and grantees (buyers).
  • Grantor signatures with names printed beneath them.
  • Two witnesses, with their names and addresses printed under their signatures.
  • A complete notary acknowledgment: names, date, notary signature, printed name, commission expiration and seal.
  • Blank space reserved at the top right corner: 3 by 3 inches on page one, 1 by 3 inches on later pages.

The clerk adds that any document transferring property needs two witnesses for each signature, though a corporation signs with its seal in place of witnesses. The sale price or consideration must appear on the deed or in a cover letter, since the clerk needs it to compute tax. The Florida statute on conveyances also asks for two subscribing witnesses on a deed of land.

How much does the Lee County clerk charge to record?

What taxes apply when a Lee County deed or mortgage is recorded?

Doc stamps come due when the deed is recorded: 70 cents for each $100, or part of $100, on warranty deeds, quit claim deeds and similar transfers. The clerk takes the money and passes it to the Department of Revenue.

Mortgages are different. The clerk's page says intangible tax on a note secured by a mortgage is paid at recording at 2 mills, or $.002 per dollar of the amount financed. The Department of Revenue adds that mortgage and note documentary stamps run 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured, with a $2,450 cap on a note and no cap on a mortgage.

On who pays, the state says all parties to a document are liable whichever one agrees to pay. Most Lee County purchase contracts assign the deed stamps to the seller, but the contract is where that gets decided. State guidance lists an estate representative's deed under a probated will as not taxable, and exempts a divorce deed for the marital home.

Does the Lee County clerk record death certificates and other documents?

Yes, with rules. The clerk says an uncertified copy of a death certificate cannot be recorded unless a court or the Attorney General deems otherwise. A Florida death certificate presented for recording must be a certified copy approved by the Department of Health that leaves out confidential cause-of-death details, and one that includes cause of death will not be recorded.

Non-Florida death certificates must be certified copies issued by that state's agencies or courts. Heirs who plan to sell a parent's Lee County house often need this paper, so order a recordable version up front. Order several copies, because the county keeps the one it records and a title company may want another for its file. Ask the Florida Department of Health, not the clerk, how to get the version that omits cause of death.

Other requirements apply to all recordings. Names must be spelled the same in the body and under each signature. Anything that moves an interest in real property, except mortgages, must show the grantee's mailing address. The page lists exceptions to these formatting rules, including wills, plats, court orders and instruments signed outside Florida. If you mail documents without a stamped return envelope, the clerk holds them, and the page says anything still held after 90 days is destroyed.

What do Lee County foreclosure and eviction filings cost, and where do they show up?

Foreclosure and other real property cases cost $470.00 below $50,000, $975.00 from $50,000 to $250,000 and $1,975.00 above $250,000 to file, according to the clerk's fee page. The clerk charges $70.00 to hold the judicial sale and asks a $600.00 deposit for the notice of sale.

A recorded lis pendens warns buyers that a suit touches the parcel. By statute the sale follows judgment by 20 to 35 days, and an electronic auction is allowed. A homeowner behind on a mortgage has the option of a pre-sale deal that clears the loan from the proceeds.

Tenant eviction filings in county court cost $185.00, and the sheriff's fee for a writ of possession is listed at $90.00, subject to change by the sheriff. Landlords selling a rented Lee County house should expect a buyer to ask for lease copies, so pull those before listing. Buyers also ask whether any tenant has received a notice, and the answer should match what the court docket shows.

How many witnesses does a Lee County deed need?

Two. The clerk's checklist calls for two witnesses with printed names and addresses, plus a full notary acknowledgment, and it adds a prepared-by statement and mailing addresses for the sellers and buyers.

Can I record an uncertified death certificate in Lee County?

No, unless a court or the Attorney General says otherwise. The certificate must be certified, and a Florida one must exclude confidential cause-of-death information.

Where are Pasco County property records kept?

The Pasco County Clerk and Comptroller keeps them, in the Official Records. Deeds, mortgages, liens and recorded civil judgments all land in that one series, and the clerk's website is the place to search it.

The clerk's FAQ says civil judgments are recorded in the county's official records, which is why a judgment against a seller can show up in a title search. Mail goes to P.O. Box 338, New Port Richey, FL 34656-0338. The FAQ gives weekday hours starting at 8:30 a.m. and ending at 5 p.m. Eastern, with holidays excluded.

Ownership and assessment data sits elsewhere. The Pasco County Property Appraiser, which counts 335,946 real property parcels, runs the records search by parcel, and its Sale Instrument Type page decodes the deed codes you see in a sales history.

The clerk's FAQ lists $10.00 for page one and $8.50 for every page after it. Those totals line up with the statute, which sets base charges of $5.00 and $4.00 and layers a trust fund charge and a $4 per page technology charge on top.

That recording charge is separate from the documentary stamp tax on a deed. State statute sets that tax at seventy cents per $100 of consideration, with Miami-Dade as the exception, and the revenue department states every party to the document is liable whoever agrees to pay. The clerk takes it at the counter as the deed goes on record.

Document size and party count can change the charge. Pasco's clerk will quote it, and Florida's statute adds $1.00 for every name beyond four. One detail matters for large documents: the statute charges an extra $1.00 per name beyond four, and a different rate for instruments larger than 14 by 8.5 inches. Ask the clerk to quote the charge before you submit anything unusual.

Most deeds do, whether or not they are recorded. The revenue department's list names warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's, life estate and deeds given in lieu of foreclosure as taxable, along with agreements for deed and certificates of title.

There are exceptions. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable, and a spousal homestead deed where the only consideration is a mortgage is exempt. The department also states that no specific exemption exists for transfers made for estate planning. A lady bird deed has its own treatment: a 2020 departmental advisement concluded that the deed in question transferred no present beneficial interest and so owed no stamp tax on those facts. Do not rely on that advisement without a closing attorney's read of your facts.

A deed must be in writing and signed in front of two subscribing witnesses, and Florida allows the witnessing by audio-video technology. A quitclaim between family members still counts as a change of ownership for assessment, which can reset a capped homestead value.

If no objection is filed, the clerk issues the certificate of title after 10 full days from the certificate of sale. It is recorded in the Official Records and transfers ownership.

On probate, the FAQ explains that probate converts assets to cash for beneficiaries and creditors and legally transfers real property. It adds that depositing a will with the clerk costs nothing. Probate cases are filed in circuit court, in the county of the decedent's home or property.

How do I protect against property fraud in Pasco County?

Sign up for the clerk's Property Fraud Alert, which watches recorded liens, deeds and mortgages in your name. You can enroll on the alert website or by phone at 800-747-4600, according to the clerk's FAQ.

If a recorded document is fraudulent, the clerk points you to the Pasco County Sheriff's Office non-emergency number, 727-847-8102.

The Property Appraiser separately takes reports of possible homestead fraud. A seller who has already left a house vacant for months can ask the clerk for the alert and keep a recent Official Records printout in the sale file.

What should I check in the records before selling a Pasco County house?

Pull the Official Records for the parcel and read every recorded item against your deed. Title companies do the same at closing, so finding a problem first gives you time to fix it.

  • Mortgages and satisfactions: is each loan paid with a recorded release?
  • Liens and judgments: civil judgments are recorded in the Official Records.
  • Tax status: ask the Pasco Tax Collector, whose recent purchases page says it is updated from ownership-change notices sent by the Property Appraiser.

Record the deed promptly after closing. The Pasco clerk's fraud alert, the Official Records search and the appraiser's sale instrument page all depend on the document being on file, and the Pasco Tax Collector updates its owner of record from ownership-change notices it receives from the appraiser. A gap between closing and recording leaves the old owner on the notices for longer.

Delinquent tax gets a certificate in June and can be auctioned after two years, per the Tax Collector, so an old unpaid bill is worth settling before you list. A recorded tax deed application is the sign that a lien has aged out.

Who keeps the property records in Sarasota County, FL?

The online search screen shows a public access group with no login. You can search by last or business name, by first name, by instrument number, by a filing date range, or by book and page. The index printed on the search screen starts on January 1, 1990.

Walk-in filing is at 1115 Manatee Avenue West, Bradenton, FL 34205, the same street address used for overnight couriers. Ordinary mail travels to a post office box: Recording, P.O. Box 25400, Bradenton, FL 34206. Phone 941-741-4045.

Section 28.222 lists what the clerk files, from deeds and claims of lien to lis pendens notices, judgments and discharge certificates. For a seller three groups matter most: the deed proving title, the mortgage and payoff trail, and any lien or judgment that could stall a closing.

What are the ways to file a document with the Manatee County clerk?

There are three ways: bring the original in person, mail it with fees and a self-addressed envelope, or submit it electronically through an approved e-recording vendor. A mailed document is recorded the day it arrives, and the clerk asks for 3 to 5 business days after that for its return.

  • Counter: originals are handed back that day.
  • Post: send fees and a stamped return envelope, with the check payable to Clerk of Circuit Court.

Legal forms and drafting help are outside the clerk's role, which points owners to an attorney or title company. Section 689.01 asks for a written conveyance signed before two witnesses. Liability falls on every party, whichever side agrees to pay, with payment made through the clerk as the deed is recorded. Manatee County follows the standard Florida rate, 70 cents on each $100 of consideration.

Consideration counts cash, a discharged debt and any mortgage on the property, assumed or not. State revenue officials treat warranty, quit claim and life estate deeds, among others, as taxable and say estate planning transfers have no dedicated exemption; a personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable.

The clerk sends tax-due questions to the Department of Revenue at 850-488-6800. Under s. 201.02(7), a spousal homestead deed funded only by a mortgage and a divorce deed for the marital home are exempt.

Owners usually get the original deed at closing from the seller or title company, and a lost one can be replaced with a recorded copy. A will is filed only after death, through Probate at 941-741-4025, a point that matters for an inherited house.

A Declaration of Domicile can be recorded with the clerk, yet the homestead exemption itself is requested from the Property Appraiser at ManateePAO.gov or 941-748-8208, with Florida's March 1 filing deadline.

The Notice of Commencement form comes from the building department that issued the permit, and the clerk lists its common charges as $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, a $1.00 per page certified copy fee with a $2.00 certification, and notary service at $5.00 for the first notarization and $2.50 for each added one.

Notary service is available at the clerk's office if you bring the completed, unsigned form and valid ID. Liens are governed by Florida Statute 713, and the clerk advises an attorney for questions. A Declaration of Domicile can be signed before a notary or in front of a deputy clerk at the Recording department, and it can be mailed or recorded in person.

For a DD-214 already recorded from 1978 to the present, only the person named can get a copy, in person with photo ID. Anyone else should contact Manatee County Veterans Services at 941-749-3030.

The clerk holds the auction and issues the deed to the top bidder. The holder of a tax certificate applies through the tax collector, and the process involves no lawsuit and no court order. The clerk's custodian of public records takes requests at 3315 Tamiami Trail East, Suite 102, Naples, FL 34112, phone (239) 252-2646.

What records does the Collier County clerk keep for a house sale?

Every instrument that has to be recorded to protect a buyer ends up in the clerk's Official Records, and a title company searches that file before a Collier County closing. Here is what you will usually find there:

  • Warranty, quit claim and other deeds that moved title to the current owner
  • Mortgages and the satisfactions that release them
  • Plat maps and condominium declarations for the subdivision or building
  • Lis pendens notices filed when a foreclosure case begins

The clerk also posts the foreclosure sale list and the tax deeds list, so a title problem tied to a court case or unpaid tax usually surfaces under one of those headings.

How much does the Collier County clerk charge to record a document?

Naples recording starts at $10.00 for page one of a letter or legal size instrument, then $8.50 per further page, per the clerk's printed schedule. How does documentary stamp tax work on a Collier County deed?

Under the revenue department's reading, each party to the document answers for the tax, whoever agrees to pay. Consideration takes in cash, a discharged debt and any mortgage on the parcel, assumed or not. Deeds are taxable whether or not they are recorded, and the same page lists warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's and life estate deeds as taxable. Mortgages and notes have their own rates. The state sets 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured, which matches the clerk's mortgage line, and caps the tax on a note at $2,450 with no cap on mortgages. Your closing agent can run the final figure.

A document counts as recorded once the clerk enters it into the Official Records. The office cannot promise same-day recording for mail or electronic submissions, so time-sensitive documents belong at the main office, where they are recorded while you wait.

The clerk charges $2.00 for a certification and $2.00 for a search per name, instrument or year, so a certified copy of a paid-off mortgage costs little compared with a delayed closing. Unpaid real estate tax turns into a tax certificate, and its holder can later seek a tax deed that the clerk auctions. The clerk's tax deeds list is the place to see which Collier parcels have reached that stage.

Under state law a tax deed application can be filed after two years have passed since April 1 of the year the certificate was issued. The county tax collector's site links to an online certificate sale. When you sell, gather the collector's payoff and the clerk's lien search side by side and give both to the closing agent. How do I research a Collier County parcel before listing?

The Collier County Property Appraiser runs the parcel search and posts public data files for the whole county or a smaller area at no charge. Pair a parcel lookup with an Official Records search by owner name, and you can match the legal description on your deed against what the appraiser shows.

Check three things before you list: the owner name spelled the same on the deed and the tax roll, any mortgage with no recorded satisfaction, and any recorded notice from a court case. A mismatch is easier to fix with the clerk before an offer arrives than during the closing week.

The rate is $0.70 per $100.00 of consideration, rounded up to the nearest hundred on the clerk's schedule. Florida makes all parties to the document liable, so the contract decides who pays it.

The Property Appraiser's site at escpa.org covers parcels in Escambia County, the City of Pensacola and the Town of Century, with values reflecting the 2026 certified roll. The Tax Collector's site lets you search a tax account by name, address or account number. Parcel data on the appraiser's site is not survey quality, so use a surveyor for boundaries.

What older records does the Escambia County Clerk hold?

The Clerk's Public Records Center keeps court, board and marriage records, plus a set of historical files that can only be viewed in person. Those historical items matter for old titles and family property.

Does the Escambia Clerk keep marriage records that affect title?

The clerk's site describes the office as the keeper of the county's Official Records. That site has a records search area, a page on researching Official Records, and a tax deed record search. The Property Appraiser keeps the parcel and ownership side, so a full picture of a house means checking both offices.   • Clerk: recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, lis pendens, tax deed files.

Where are Osceola County property records kept?

Deeds and mortgages for Osceola County end up at one counter: the clerk who also serves as county comptroller and recorder. The county government site describes the clerk's duties as split between clerk of the circuit and county courts and county recorder, and it points residents to osceolaclerk.com for recording forms, eRecording, tax deeds and property fraud alerting.

The clerk's FAQ explains that everything recordable goes into a single running series labeled the Official Records. The series is permanent and a record leaves it only by court order. A separate office, the Property Appraiser, sits at 2505 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Kissimmee, and it handles parcel values and exemptions.

What documents does the Osceola clerk record?

The clerk records deeds, leases, mortgages, liens, judgments and many other instruments that touch real or personal property. The clerk's FAQ lists several kinds, drawn from state law.

  • Deeds, mortgages, notices or claims of lien, and their releases and satisfactions
  • Notices of lis pendens, which warn that a lawsuit affects a property
  • Judgments and their assignments, releases and satisfactions
  • Federal tax liens and certificates that release them
  • Certified death certificates and military discharge records

For a seller, the lis pendens and the judgment entries deserve a look. A pending foreclosure case will show up as a lis pendens against the parcel, and a recorded judgment can attach to land you own.

What are the Osceola County recording requirements for a deed?

A deed must meet the clerk's formal checklist or it can be rejected until corrected. The clerk's page cites Florida Statute 695.26 and lists what the face of the document needs.

  • The grantor's signature notarized, with name and address printed below it
  • Two witnesses, with printed names; for documents on or after January 1, 2024, witness post office addresses too
  • A complete legal description of the property
  • The grantee's mailing address and the preparer's name and address, using a person's first and last name and not just a business name
  • A 3 by 3 inch blank space at the top right corner for the clerk's use
  • Original ink signatures, since photocopies are refused

Title searches are not a clerk service; the office refers people to title agencies and attorneys.

Report it, because the clerk cannot pull a filing without a court order. The same page says that section 817.535 of the Florida Statutes makes recording a fraudulent instrument against property a third degree felony, and that a court may order a fraudulent document voided and removed. What do Osceola tax records and tax deeds mean for a sale?

Unpaid real estate tax in Osceola becomes delinquent at the start of April and picks up a 3 percent addition. Certificates for those parcels are auctioned online by June 1, and bids begin at 18 percent and fall.

The clerk holds tax deed sales online. A certificate left alone can support a tax deed application from April 1 of the second year after purchase. On the clerk's page, the winner forfeits a deposit if they walk away, set at the greater of 5 percent of the bid or $200, and has a day to deliver the balance. Tax deed land is sold as is, and the clerk warns that it carries no promise of clear title.

Overbid money after a sale can be claimed with an affidavit sent to the clerk's Tax Deed Department.

What dates matter on an Osceola County tax bill?

The Osceola County Tax Collector's calendar runs on a few fixed dates. Payments open in November at a 4 percent discount, stepping to 3, 2 and 1 percent through February, with the gross amount owed in March.

New requests to join the quarterly installment plan must be in by April 30. Installments then fall on June 30, September 30 and December 31. An installment that misses July 31 loses its discount, adds a 5 percent penalty and ends the plan.

  • Three weeks of newspaper advertising before the certificate sale

Before 4:30 p.m. on a business day. The office stays open until 5:00 p.m., but recording stops at 4:30, and later documents are recorded the next business day.
